newsitem.title: EGYPT: Dogs, computers search for living in Cairo collapse.
newsitem.headline: Dogs, computers search for living in Cairo collapse.

text.p: Rescuers used dogs and computers on Thursday in a race against time to find any survivors entombed for days in the debris of a collapsed Cairo apartment block in which at least 32 people have died.

On their first day at the site, Hungarian Civil Defence workers unleashed their sniffer dogs and Japan's Disaster Relief Team poked state-of-the-art computerised detectors into the cavernous centre of the 11-storey building which fell on Sunday.

"Now we're removing ceilings on the top of the heap to find any alive (people) on the stairs because people ran on the stairs and they were in the middle of the building," Major Ayman Samak of the Egyptian Fire Brigade told Reuters.
"We have a lot of teams working with us now," Samak said. "Until we finish the building, we always have hope, a big hope. We don't lose hope for live people."
Dozens of people are still missing and believed buried under the rubble.
More than 20 survivors have been dug from the rubble but rescuers say four died later in hospital. On Tuesday, two women were pulled out alive after 36 hours entombed in the rubble.

"We have a Hungarian team with special dogs capable of finding people under the rubble. If there are some people alive, the dogs are very clever and will find them," Mihaly Szabo, Hungary's deputy head of mission, said.
Demolition workers hammered and chiselled to penetrate a concrete layer five ceilings thick to the stairwell.

The rescuers thought of the atrium after the 24-strong Japanese and German Red Cross volunteers said the only corner of the building that did not fully collapse was empty of both survivors and corpses.
"Maybe inside the house there is like a cave and there are survivors. There is nothing outside," a Hungarian rescuer said.
Authorities said the building had been illegally heightened and have charged its owner with manslaughter and building without a licence, Cairo newspapers said. He faces up to 10 years in jail.
They reported that the committee in charge of investigating the collapse were almost sure renovation work in one of the building's flats had knocked down a few columns and destabilised the structure.
Officials have promised tougher punishments for unlicensed buildings and parliament is expected to discuss drafting a law banning people from renovating flats without expert permission.

Soaring property prices have encouraged landlords to add extra floors illegally. Several buildings have collapsed beneath the extra weight and recent earthquakes have also taken their toll on poorly constructed buildings in the crowded Egyptian capital.
